record_identity.title: New Mexico lawyer filed ChatGPT-assisted appellate brief containing fabricated witnesses and testimony

incident_identity.historical_event_name: 2026 State v. Sandoval ChatGPT-fabricated appellate brief incident
incident_identity.date_basis: The reviewed public sources do not establish the exact date on which the brief in chief was filed. September 9, 2026 is the date of the New Mexico Supreme Court dispositional order and is retained only as a reported-date fallback, not as an asserted filing date.

summary: The Supreme Court of New Mexico found attorney Stephen D. Aarons in direct contempt after he acknowledged using ChatGPT in preparing a criminal appellate brief that contained false testimony from wholly fabricated witnesses, false testimony attributed to real witnesses, and misrepresentations of legal authority. The court recorded that Aarons admitted he did not verify the factual claims or legal authority before signing and filing the brief. The court struck the briefing, appointed the Law Office of the Public Defender for the defendant-appellant, ordered new briefing, imposed a $5,000 sanction payable to the State Bar Client Protection Fund, referred Aarons to the Disciplinary Board, and barred him from appearing before the court pending disciplinary proceedings. Reuters independently reported the order and Aarons's statement that he had used ChatGPT to summarize trial proceedings and had not understood the degree of hallucination risk.

vigil_assessment.factual_basis: The New Mexico Supreme Court's September 9, 2026 dispositional order states that Stephen D. Aarons acknowledged using ChatGPT to prepare the brief in chief, admitted that the brief included false testimony from wholly fabricated witnesses and false testimony attributed to real witnesses, admitted that it misrepresented legal authority, and admitted that he did not verify the factual claims or legal authority before signing and filing it. The order records direct contempt, disciplinary referral, a temporary bar on appearances before the court, striking of all briefing, appointment of replacement counsel, new briefing, and a $5,000 sanction. Reuters independently reports the same core occurrence and quotes Aarons as saying he used ChatGPT to summarize trial proceedings.
vigil_assessment.governance_interpretation: The occurrence combines two independently evidenced verification-and-reliance failures. First, generated factual and legal material was propagated into a criminal appellate filing despite not meeting the epistemic assurance required for a reliance-bearing judicial artefact. Second, the required verification step was expressly omitted: the court records the attorney's admission that he did not verify the factual claims or legal authority before filing. The record does not treat ChatGPT as the sole causal actor; professional reliance and verification decisions were made by the filing attorney.
vigil_assessment.significance_to_cam: The incident demonstrates a concrete boundary between generative assistance and reliance-bearing professional use. A model output may be useful for drafting or summarisation while remaining unfit for formal evidentiary or legal reliance until the factual record and cited authority are independently verified. Where a human or agent promotes generated material into an institutional artefact, the assurance threshold must follow the downstream use rather than the convenience of the generation step.
assessment_boundaries: The exact filing date of the brief is not established in the reviewed public sources; September 9, 2026 is the date of the court's dispositional order.
The reviewed sources identify the product as ChatGPT but do not establish the model or runtime version used.
VIGIL did not review the underlying ChatGPT conversation or independently reconstruct which fabricated statements originated directly from model output versus later human editing.

The court order establishes the attorney's admitted failure to verify and the filing defects; VIGIL does not determine any further professional-discipline outcome beyond the referral and temporary appearance bar recorded in the order.
The occurrence is not treated as evidence that all AI-assisted legal drafting is unreliable or that model use itself constitutes misconduct.
